questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of corporate culture?
options: The shared values, beliefs and ways of working in an organisation
The organisational structure shown on a business chart
The written rules and procedures staff must follow
The published mission statement of a business
questions.why: Culture is the shared values, beliefs, attitudes and ways of working: how things are done when nobody is watching.
whyNot: That is structure, which is formal and written down; culture is unwritten.
Rules are a formal system; a strong culture reduces the need for them.
A mission statement is what a business says; culture is what it actually does.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a strong corporate culture?
options: One whose values are widely shared and deeply held by employees
One that is enforced through strict rules and close supervision
One created by a business with a long history
One that produces high profits
questions.why: Strength refers to how widely and deeply values are shared, not to how strictly behaviour is policed.
whyNot: Relying on rules and supervision is a sign of a weak culture, not a strong one.
Age helps a culture form but does not by itself make it shared or deeply held.
Profit is an outcome; a strong culture pointing the wrong way can damage profit.

questions.stem: Which of Handy's cultures concentrates authority in one person or a small group?
options: Power culture
Role culture
Task culture
Person culture
questions.why: In a power culture authority sits with one individual or a small central group, so decisions are fast and depend on that person being right.
whyNot: A role culture bases authority on position and procedure rather than on an individual.
A task culture organises around project teams where expertise matters more than rank.
A person culture is one where individuals see themselves as more important than the organisation.

questions.stem: Which of Handy's cultures is based on clear job descriptions, procedures and hierarchy?
options: Role culture
Power culture
Task culture
Person culture
questions.why: In a role culture authority comes from your position, and the business runs on defined roles and procedures.
whyNot: A power culture depends on an individual rather than on defined roles.
A task culture is built around temporary project teams, not fixed job descriptions.
A person culture has little shared structure at all.

questions.stem: Which of Handy's cultures organises work around project teams assembled for a specific purpose?
options: Task culture
Role culture
Power culture
Person culture
questions.why: A task culture brings together the expertise needed for a project and disbands the team afterwards, which is why it suits a matrix structure.
whyNot: A role culture uses permanent departments and fixed procedures.
A power culture centres on an individual, not on teams.
A person culture exists to serve the individuals in it rather than any shared task.

questions.stem: A group of lawyers share premises and support staff but each regards the practice as existing to serve their own work. Which culture is this?
options: Person culture
Task culture
Role culture
Power culture
questions.why: Person culture is where individuals see themselves as superior to the organisation, which is common among professionals sharing facilities.
whyNot: A task culture has a shared project purpose, which is exactly what is missing here.
A role culture has hierarchy and procedures directing the individuals.
A power culture has a dominant central figure, which is not described.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the strongest single influence in forming a corporate culture?
options: Who gets rewarded and promoted
The wording of the mission statement
The number of levels in the hierarchy
The size of the marketing budget
questions.why: Staff learn what the business really values from who succeeds in it, so the reward and promotion system is the strongest signal of all.
whyNot: A statement is only words; if behaviour contradicts it, staff follow the behaviour.
Structure influences culture but does not determine the values people hold.
The marketing budget affects external image rather than internal values.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a disadvantage of a strong corporate culture?
options: It can produce groupthink and resistance to change
It increases the need for supervision and rules
It makes recruitment decisions harder
It always reduces employee motivation
questions.why: Widely shared values make change harder and can suppress dissenting views, so a strong culture pointing the wrong way is worse than a weak one.
whyNot: A strong culture reduces the need for supervision, because staff know how to behave.
It makes recruitment easier, because there is a clear idea of fit; the cost is less diversity of thought.
A strong culture usually raises motivation; its problems lie in rigidity.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a weak corporate culture?
options: One where values are not widely shared, so behaviour depends on rules and supervision
One held by a business that is performing badly
One in a business with few employees
One in which employees are poorly paid
questions.why: Weakness is about how little the values are shared, which means behaviour has to be directed rather than assumed.
whyNot: Poor performance may have many causes and a weak culture may still perform adequately.
Small businesses often have very strong cultures, usually set by the founder.
Pay levels are a reward issue, not a measure of cultural strength.

questions.stem: A business announces new values emphasising teamwork but continues to promote the most individually aggressive managers. What is the most likely outcome?
options: Staff will conclude the real culture still rewards individual aggression
The culture will change because the values have been formally stated
Teamwork will improve because the announcement raises awareness
The promoted managers will adopt the new values first
questions.why: Culture follows rewards rather than statements, so the promotion decisions tell staff what the business actually values.
whyNot: A statement does not change beliefs; staff test it against what they observe.
Awareness without any change in consequences rarely changes behaviour.
Those who gained under the old system have the least reason to change.

questions.stem: Why is middle management often the strongest source of resistance to culture change?
options: Their authority came from the old way of working, so they have most to lose
They have the least contact with senior management
They are usually the lowest paid group in the business
They have no influence over how change is implemented
questions.why: Middle managers often derive their status and authority from existing procedures and hierarchy, so a new culture threatens their position directly.
whyNot: Contact with senior management is not the issue; loss of status is.
Middle managers are not the lowest paid group, and pay is not the cause here.
They have considerable influence, which is precisely why their resistance matters so much.

questions.stem: A cross-border acquisition underperforms badly. Which explanation is most commonly given?
options: Culture clash between the two workforces
The purchase price was paid in the wrong currency
The acquirer had too few shareholders
The target had a written mission statement
questions.why: Culture clash is the most common single cause of acquisition failure, because two workforces with different attitudes to hierarchy and decision-making do not merge just because a contract was signed.
whyNot: Currency of payment affects cost, not the long-run performance of the combined business.
The number of shareholders does not explain integration failure.
A mission statement is unrelated to whether the two cultures can work together.

questions.stem: A business with a deeply procedural role culture adopts a strategy requiring fast, innovative decisions. What is the most likely problem?
options: The organisation will be unable to execute the strategy even if the strategy is sound
The strategy will succeed because structure is irrelevant to execution
The role culture will change automatically to fit the new strategy
The business will become a person culture
questions.why: Strategy has to fit the culture, or the culture has to change first, and culture change takes years while the strategy usually needs results sooner.
whyNot: Culture directly shapes how decisions are made, so it is central to execution.
Culture does not adapt automatically; it is unwritten and reinforced by existing rewards.
Person culture is unrelated to this situation and would not follow from a new strategy.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most effective way to change a corporate culture?
options: Change what gets rewarded and promoted, and lead visibly and consistently
Publish a new set of values on the company website
Send all employees an email explaining the new culture
Raise pay across the business
questions.why: Because culture follows consequences rather than announcements, changing the reward and promotion system, backed by consistent leadership behaviour, is what actually shifts it.
whyNot: Published values are only a claim, and staff judge it against behaviour.
One communication does not change deeply held shared beliefs.
A pay rise may improve satisfaction temporarily without changing shared values.

questions.stem: Why is corporate culture so difficult to change quickly?
options: It is unwritten, held by people, and reinforced by past success
It is protected by employment law in most countries
It is recorded in the statement of financial position
It can only be changed by shareholders at a general meeting
questions.why: There is no document to amend: the culture is in the beliefs and habits of the people, and past success is a powerful argument for keeping it.
whyNot: No law prevents a business changing how it works; the barrier is behavioural.
Culture is an intangible that does not appear in the financial statements.
Shareholders do not vote on culture; it emerges from behaviour inside the business.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best evaluative point about culture in a 20-mark question?
options: A strong culture is an asset or a liability depending on whether it points in the right direction
Culture is always more important than strategy
Every business should aim for a task culture
Culture can be measured accurately from the annual accounts
questions.why: The judgement is conditional: strength itself is neutral, and its value depends on whether the shared values suit the market the business is in.
whyNot: Neither dominates in all cases; the examinable point is that they must fit each other.
The best culture depends on the industry; safety-critical work needs procedure, not loose project teams.
Culture is non-financial and does not appear in the accounts, which is one of their limitations.
